title: Purkinje Cells
intro: Purkinje cells are the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex and among the largest neurons in the brain. Each has a fan-shaped, nearly flat dendritic tree that receives on the order of 100,000 to 200,000 parallel fibre synapses in rodent (more in human) and a single climbing fibre that wraps its main dendrites. They fire two completely different kinds of spike, and they are inhibitory: everything the cerebellar cortex computes leaves it as a pattern of GABAergic inhibition onto the deep nuclei.

items: Morphology: a large soma in the Purkinje cell layer, a thick primary dendrite branching into a dense, planar tree in the molecular layer, perpendicular to the parallel fibres so that each parallel fibre crosses many Purkinje cells but contacts each only once or twice.

Simple spikes: ordinary sodium spikes fired spontaneously at high rates (about 30 to 100 Hz in vivo, even without input) thanks to resurgent sodium current and fast potassium currents (Raman & Bean 1997). Parallel fibre input and molecular layer interneuron inhibition raise or lower this rate.

Complex spikes: when the climbing fibre fires, its hundreds of synapses produce a massive, all-or-none depolarisation, a burst of a large spike followed by several small spikelets and a dendritic calcium spike, lasting about 5 to 10 ms. Complex spikes occur at about 1 Hz.
Dendritic calcium: P-type (Cav2.1) calcium channels are dense in the dendrites; climbing fibre input produces widespread dendritic calcium spikes, the trigger for plasticity.

Bistability: in slices and some in vivo conditions Purkinje cells show up and down states of firing, toggled by complex spikes (Loewenstein et al. 2005), though how common this is in awake animals is debated.

Plasticity: parallel fibre LTD when parallel fibre and climbing fibre activity coincide; parallel fibre LTP without climbing fibre activity; plasticity of inhibitory inputs and intrinsic excitability as well.

De Schutter and Bower (1994): the landmark detailed Purkinje cell model, with 1,600 compartments from a reconstructed guinea-pig cell and ten channel types distributed between soma and dendrite. It reproduces simple spikes, dendritic calcium spikes and complex spikes, and showed that background inhibition and excitation keep the dendrite in a responsive regime. One of the most cited models in computational neuroscience.
Khaliq, Gouwens and Raman (2003): a single-compartment model built around the resurgent sodium current, explaining high-frequency spontaneous firing.

Akemann and Knopfel (2006), Masoli et al. (2015) and Zang, Dieudonne and De Schutter (2018): updated detailed models with modern channel data; Zang et al. reproduce the dendritic responses to climbing fibre and parallel fibre input and the variability of complex spike waveforms.
Reduced models: two-compartment Purkinje models that capture simple and complex spikes, and Izhikevich-style or AdEx point models with intrinsic pacemaking for networks.

Computational abstractions: the perceptron (Marr 1969; Albus 1971); Brunel et al. (2004) computed the optimal storage capacity of a Purkinje cell as a perceptron with sign-constrained excitatory weights and found that most synapses should be silent at capacity, as observed (Isope & Barbour 2002). Clopath and Brunel (2013) extended the analysis to perceptrons with analog (firing-rate) outputs, and Clopath et al. (2014) used the theory in a model of vestibulo-ocular reflex learning.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: A Purkinje-like readout is a perceptron with a high baseline rate that inputs push up or down; it is trained by a separate, sparse teaching signal (the climbing fibre) rather than by its own output.
Implement climbing-fibre-gated plasticity as a three-factor rule: parallel fibre trace × climbing fibre spike → depression; parallel fibre activity alone → slow potentiation.
Expect most weights to go to zero after learning; this is predicted by perceptron theory and is what real Purkinje cells show.
This is a different style of learning from a cortical column's unsupervised STDP: useful when your system has an explicit error signal, such as motor control or prediction correction.
